lessonTitle: Post-Marketing Safety Monitoring: Reports, Registries and Signals

blocks.text: A new anti-inflammatory is licensed after trials in 3500 patients, none of whom developed liver failure. Within two years of marketing, doctors across the country notice six cases among 800 000 users. The trials were not wrong; they simply could not have seen an event that rare. Safety knowledge is incomplete on the day a drug is licensed.

blocks.markdown: Before licensing, a drug's safety is studied in randomised trials. These are essential but limited: they enrol a few hundred to a few thousand patients, follow them for months, apply strict inclusion and exclusion criteria (often excluding older adults, pregnant women, children, people with multiple conditions and those on many other drugs) and monitor closely. Rare reactions, delayed reactions and reactions in excluded groups can therefore be missed. **Post-marketing surveillance** is monitoring the safety of the drug once it is used in the wider population.

blocks.caption: Rule of three: if no event is seen in n patients, the true event rate could plausibly be as high as 3/n, with 95% confidence.

blocks.title: What does 'no cases seen' exclude?
blocks.prompt: In a trial of 2400 patients no case of a serious skin reaction occurred. What is the largest event rate the trial cannot exclude, and how many patients would be needed to be reasonably sure of seeing at least one case of an event of incidence 1 in 5000?

steps.text: Apply the rule of three to the first question.
This is about 1 in 800, so a reaction with incidence 1 in 1000 could easily have been missed.
For an event of incidence 1/5000, about 3 expected cases give a 95% chance of at least one.

blocks.answer: Up to about 1 in 800 cannot be excluded; roughly 15 000 exposed patients are needed to see a 1-in-5000 event.

rows: Everyone treated, including older adults and complex patients
blocks.caption: Trials versus surveillance.

blocks.markdown: **Yellow card style schemes.** In the United Kingdom, clinicians and patients send **spontaneous reports** of suspected adverse reactions to the regulator (the Yellow Card scheme, begun in the 1960s after thalidomide). Similar national schemes exist elsewhere. The strengths are that the whole population is covered for the lifetime of the drug, new reactions can be noticed early, and unusual events can be flagged. The limitations are **under-reporting**, variable quality, and the lack of a denominator, so spontaneous reports cannot give true incidence and are subject to reporting bias, such as publicity driving reports.

Other tools complement spontaneous reports: **registries** of patients with a given condition or exposure (for example pregnancy registries), **cohort studies** and **case-control studies** using electronic health records, and **prescription-event monitoring**, which follows up prescribers about patients given a new drug. These can estimate incidence and compare with unexposed patients.

**Signals.** A **safety signal** is information suggesting a possible new causal association between a drug and an adverse event, or a new aspect of a known one, that justifies further investigation. Statistical screening of report databases often uses **disproportionality**: whether a reaction is reported more often with one drug than with others. A common measure is the proportional reporting ratio (PRR).

blocks.caption: a: reports of the reaction with the drug; b: reports of other reactions with the drug; c: reports of the reaction with all other drugs; d: reports of other reactions with all other drugs.

blocks.title: Calculating a proportional reporting ratio
blocks.prompt: Among 500 reports for drug X, 20 are for hepatitis. Among 20 000 reports for all other drugs, 100 are for hepatitis. Calculate the PRR.

steps.text: Proportion of hepatitis among drug X reports.

blocks.answer: PRR is 8: hepatitis is reported eight times more often proportionally with drug X. This is a signal to investigate, not proof of causation.

rows: Case review, timing, dechallenge, mechanism, trial data
Does the drug cause it, and how often?
blocks.caption: From signal to confirmed adverse drug reaction.

blocks.title: Signal is not proof
blocks.text: A signal is a hypothesis generated from reports; it becomes a confirmed adverse drug reaction only after evaluation shows a causal relationship. High reporting ratios can arise from publicity, confounding by indication or channelling.

points: Trials are limited by size, duration and selected patients, so rare, delayed and special-population adverse effects may only appear after marketing; the rule of three quantifies what zero events excludes.
Yellow card style schemes collect spontaneous reports from the whole population but suffer from under-reporting and lack of a denominator; registries and cohort studies add incidence data.
A signal is a hypothesis flagged by reports or statistics; it is confirmed as an adverse drug reaction only after causality is established.

questions.stem: Which is the main reason clinical trials may fail to detect rare adverse effects?

options.text: Small numbers, limited duration and selected patients
Trials are never conducted in humans
Regulators ignore trial data
Placebo groups always mask adverse effects

questions.correctOptionText: Small numbers, limited duration and selected patients

distractorRationale.c: Regulators review trial data in detail.
distractorRationale.d: Placebo groups help to identify, not mask, attributable effects.

questions.explanation: A rare event may simply not occur in a few thousand patients followed for a limited time, and high-risk groups are often excluded. Post-marketing surveillance extends observation to the wider population.

questions.stem: A trial of 4000 patients finds no cases of a serious liver reaction. Using the rule of three, which conclusion is appropriate?

options.text: The incidence could still be as high as about 1 in 1300, so rarer events may have been missed
The drug has been proven to be completely safe for the liver
The incidence must be exactly zero
The true incidence is at least 1 in 4000

questions.correctOptionText: The incidence could still be as high as about 1 in 1300, so rarer events may have been missed

distractorRationale.b: Zero observed events does not prove zero risk.
distractorRationale.c: Absence of events does not mean exactly zero.
distractorRationale.d: Zero observed events do not set a lower bound.

questions.explanation: The rule of three gives an upper 95% limit of 3/n, here 0.075%. Larger populations or longer follow-up are needed to detect rarer events.

questions.stem: The Yellow Card scheme is an example of which type of safety monitoring?

options.text: Spontaneous reporting
Randomised controlled trial
Cross-sectional prevalence survey
Genome sequencing

questions.explanation: Clinicians and patients voluntarily report suspected adverse reactions, which allows continuous monitoring across the whole treated population.

questions.stem: Why can spontaneous reports alone not be used to calculate the incidence of an adverse reaction?

options.text: Under-reporting and the lack of a denominator of exposed patients
Reports are always inaccurate
Regulators do not read them
They contain no information about drugs

questions.correctOptionText: Under-reporting and the lack of a denominator of exposed patients

distractorRationale.b: Reports can be accurate but incomplete.

questions.explanation: Only a fraction of events is reported and the number of people exposed is not known, so the numerator and denominator are both uncertain.

questions.stem: Twenty-two reports of tendon rupture have been received for a recently marketed antibiotic and a disproportionality analysis gives a high ratio. How should this be described?

options.text: A safety signal requiring evaluation, not yet a confirmed adverse reaction
A proven adverse drug reaction
A random artefact to be ignored
An incidence figure

questions.correctOptionText: A safety signal requiring evaluation, not yet a confirmed adverse reaction

distractorRationale.b: Causality has not yet been established.
distractorRationale.c: A high ratio should be investigated, not ignored.
distractorRationale.d: A reporting ratio is not an incidence.

questions.explanation: A signal is a hypothesis. Evaluation of case details, plausibility, trial data and epidemiology is needed before it becomes a confirmed adverse drug reaction.

questions.stem: A proportional reporting ratio greater than 1 proves that the drug caused the reaction.

options.text: True
False

questions.explanation: It shows only that the reaction is reported proportionally more often with the drug. Publicity, channelling and confounding can raise the ratio without causation.

questions.stem: A phase III trial of 1500 patients records no cases of a serious reaction. Using the rule of three, calculate the upper 95% limit of the event rate as a percentage.
questions.explanation: The upper limit is 3 divided by 1500, which equals 0.002, or 0.2%. A reaction as common as 1 in 500 therefore cannot be excluded.

questions.stem: For drug Y there are 12 reports of pancreatitis among 400 reports for the drug, and 150 pancreatitis reports among 30 000 reports for all other drugs. Calculate the proportional reporting ratio.
questions.explanation: The proportion for drug Y is 12/400 = 0.03 and for others is 150/30 000 = 0.005. The ratio is 0.03/0.005, which equals 6, a signal to evaluate.

questions.stem: Explain, with numerical reasoning, why a trial of 3000 patients in which no serious reaction was seen cannot prove a drug is safe. Give two other reasons trials may miss adverse effects.
markingGuide: Rule of three: upper 95% limit is about 3/3000, which is 1 in 1000
Number of patients needed for rarer events is larger, for example about 3 divided by incidence
Selected populations exclude older adults, pregnant women or those with multiple drugs
Controlled monitoring differs from routine care
questions.explanation: Absence of evidence in a small sample is not evidence of absence. Marking should reward the quantitative reasoning and at least two further reasons.

questions.stem: Describe the role, strengths and limitations of national Yellow Card style schemes, and explain how a signal from such reports is distinguished from a confirmed adverse drug reaction.
markingGuide: Spontaneous voluntary reports to the regulator
Strengths: whole population, long-term, early detection, rare events
Limitations: under-reporting, no denominator, reporting bias
Signal: possible new causal association needing investigation
Evaluation by case review, plausibility, trial and epidemiological data
Confirmation when causality is established, then regulatory action
questions.explanation: Spontaneous reports generate hypotheses. Confirmation needs further evidence, and marking should reward this distinction.
